utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it's been suggested to me that you wish to raise some issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it's something I need to discuss in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because this concerns materials received from Serbia for which a request was made that we not use them in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, the challenges to the expert report of -- of Radinovic are fairly limited, and they are very clearly expressed. Can they be answered today? If the answer to that -- if the answer to that is "no," then they'll have to be dealt with early tomorrow morning. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Sepenuk will take this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, I don't think -- I just received that -- I just looked at that last night for the first time. And I don't think that General Radinovic is a practical matter. I mean, I'm not even sure when General Krga will be through. But as a practical matter, General Radinovic particularly because of these intercepts really can't testify on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, Curcin will be through tomorrow, and we have a decision to take about Radinovic, so everyone knows the position when we come back if he's not giving evidence tomorrow. As things stand. The rest is speculation. The challenges are very clear and should be capable of being dealt with very quickly. We're in this position because you didn't produce your report at the time you should have produced it, and therefore we're not inclined to be conceding more and more time at this stage. It has to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think it would be best then, Your Honour, to do it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And that will impinge on your own time for your witnesses, and you have to bear that in mind as well. I was giving you the opportunity to do it in writing to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's your choice. Now, Mr. Ivetic, are you likely to have anything to say about this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from seeking cross-examination on -- of the witness, that's all I would say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So you oppose the position of it as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As it stands, no, with the ability of cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we return to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the delay, but we were dealing with matters of law and administrative matters that were of urgency and had to be attended to just now. So we're sorry for keeping you waiting. Your examination by Mr. Visnjic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, before this Tribunal lieutenant colonel of the Yugoslav Army Djorovic testified, and in his statement P2671, in paragraph 6, he stated that on the 30th of December, 2003, he gave an expose at a forum consisting of about 100 officers, and because of that speech of his, it turned out to be his last working day in the Ministry of Defence. An order was issued that he be transferred to the post of a legal desk officer in Belgrade, in the Belgrade Corps command, and at a meeting attended by General Krga, the chief of the legal administration and General Zivanovic, he says: "I was informed I had been punished and that I should go back to the legal administration. I appealed against this order, but to this day no decision has been reached."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If I may enquire: I know Mr. Djorovic's statement was listed as a potential exhibit. But I didn't see in the 65 ter summary of this witness's evidence that he was going to talk about this matter. Is it in there someplace that I've missed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe so, Your Honours, but if Mr. Hannis feels it's a major problem for him, I will withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I wasn't prepared for it. I see that it is item number 104 in his list of exhibits, but there was no reference to Mr. Djorovic in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is not a peripheral a matter, well depending on the question, but the evidence of Djorovic is of some significance and therefore we would be inclined, I think, to hear evidence that bears on that and then to allow some other remedy to you, Mr. Hannis if you're prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, but if it is of pertinence, it should have been in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I -- I entirely agree. And Mr. Visnjic, I'm sure, realises that -- I don't think there's any ill-will involved in these exchanges, Mr. Hannis. I think it's been difficult for Mr. Visnjic because of the way in which they've put this together perhaps in the latter stages of preparation to get absolutely everything into these. Some of them seem to be longer than the evidence of the witness in the end of the day. So it's not for want of, I think, goodwill that these blips occur. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us something about the incident I've just read about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic and General Zivanovic were in my office one day and we discussed his status. On that occasion, he put forward his own view of this affair. I ordered that -- or instructed, rather, that everything that could be done be done and that his status be resolved pursuant to the law. However, you said that afterwards he was punished by the security organ. I don't think that's correct because the security organs were not those who imposed sanctions on members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the meeting you attended, was he informed that the organs of military security had punished him, as he said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, that couldn't have happened. He couldn't have been informed of that, because the security organs have no right to punish anyone. That's according to the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, when was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really cannot really recall the date when that happened. It's very hard to remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose was -- well, he asked that I, as chief of the General Staff, receive him, for him to tell me about his status problems. At the time, he was in the command of the Belgrade Corps and the Belgrade Corps was subordinate to me, so that I was his second in command and he had a right to ask me -- or rather, his second superior - interpreter's correction - and he had a right to correct a meeting with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was he complaining about his removal from his post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He felt that the position given to him did not correspond to his merits, his professional ability, and so on and so forth. He requested that he be appointed colonel, and according to our law, for someone to be appointed colonel, they had to complete certain courses or certain training. If they had civilian education, they had to have a masters degree, or if they went to the command staff school, they would have to have a certain degree also. But he had neither of those requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let's go back to, so to speak, more serious topics. In 1999 in the activities of the Army of Yugoslavia in 1999, was moving the civilian population ever an aim?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really not. I never saw that in any document, nor did I ever attend any meeting at which someone put forward such an idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you attended many meetings and participated in peace negotiations also. In any of those situations, was an option considered of moving the civilian population of Albanian ethnicity or their expulsion or their retention in Albania in order to improve the ethnic balance in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate, I never heard such ideas at any of the meeting I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you were the chief of the General Staff and you know what is possible from that position. Do you know whether General Ojdanic in his activities in the period while you collaborated with him, from 1999 onwards, contributed in any way to the deterioration of the situation or the bringing of Yugoslavia into a war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, General Ojdanic on various occasions before the war said that war would be the worst possible outcome for us, that it would cause us enormous damage, and he did his utmost to find ways of avoiding war. I think that in his activities he did not contribute to or incite in any way the processes that led to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, one more question. Did the Army of Yugoslavia ever consider that the Kosovo issue can be solved by military means, through the military option?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we considered the problem of Kosovo and Metohija, we always considered several scenarios, and almost always the conclusion was that absolutely the best way would be to solve this through peaceful means. Of course, we assumed that the war option might ensue, and so we carried out certain preparations that any responsible army would carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A very short cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. General, as far as you know, was a meeting ever held of the Supreme Defence Council after the 23rd of March, 1999? So I'm talking about the wartime period up until the 10th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings of the Supreme Defence Council would usually be announced in advance, and then press releases would be issued. That -- those meetings were held, and what conclusions were reached. As far as I can remember, there were no such meetings or such sessions in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear anything else, any other information from any other source that any such meetings were held in that period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I received no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, in the course of this trial, we heard the term "Supreme Command" used, being used. We know that the Constitution and the relevant legal regulations - I'm referring to the law on the army and on defence - do not recognise this term, but it was -- its use was not debatable. But could you please tell me, what did you understand? Who were members of the Supreme Command? If you can tell us. How did you understand that term?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you said yourself, our Constitution and our laws do not recognise this term. This term is not used. And I didn't really concern myself with its meaning. It is possible that it means different things for different people, but I really did not concern myself with that, with the meaning of the word "Supreme Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, who were the members of the Supreme Command, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the Supreme Command was not defined in our laws, there can be differing views as to what it was supposed to do. My belief is that it existed and that it should have included members of the Supreme Defence Council, the Prime Minister, the Defence Minister, the Minister of the Interior, the Finance Minister possibly, and perhaps some other high-ranking officials of the state. And as we know, this was not the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. My name is Djuro Cepic and I'm representing Vladimir Lazerevic. Before I ask my first question, could we please have the Exhibit 3D782 in e-court. General, this document that you will now see on your screen was shown to you by my learned colleague Mr. Visnjic, and the first sentence reads: "Some information indicates that NATO is planning to intimidate the civilian population by airstrikes and so cause a major exodus over the next seven to ten days to the centre of Serbia, Albania, and Macedonia." Did you have any information that great movements of people followed in those directions, in particular towards Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained already how we obtained this information. And as for the movements of people out of Kosovo and Metohija to various -- in various directions, I think that it is quite a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in line 5 - that's line 5 in Serbian -- or rather, in B/C/S - it says: "which will enable them to mount defensive airstrikes with the use of chemical agents." The use of chemical agents. General, do you know that the units that were on the ground sent reports that some unknown liquids were used, that they were targeted with those unknown -- unidentified liquids?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were reports of some fireballs being observed, that weapons containing depleted uranium were used, but I don't recall any reports of the use of chemical agents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 3D898, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the last words in the first paragraph, this is something that my colleague Mr. Visnjic addressed yesterday. He asked you about the EC-130 aircraft. And I'm more interested in the A-10 Thunder Bolt Aircraft, as it is designated here. Do you know what kind of ammunition is used by this plane? And you indicated that this plane might be used on the 28th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A-10 aeroplanes are used to provide -- provide immediate support to ground forces. Among other things, it carries 30-millimetre rounds containing depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in the e-court system Exhibit Number 5D345, please. I'm afraid that we haven't got translation for this document, so I will ask the witness just to read one sentence. Oh, hopefully we will have translation. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in the bottom part of the document, do you recognise the stamp and the signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, that's General Lazarevic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And do you see from the heading that it pertains to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the way that the documents coming from Pristina Corps were marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first sentence. The use and engagement of about 60 A-10 planes. So does that confirm the information that you provided in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not only that information, but many other reports confirm that those planes had been deployed in several locations in Kosovo and Metohija, but also in the southern parts of Central Serbia. In the post-war period, we decontaminated four areas in the sector between Presevo [phoen] and Vranjevo [phoen], where we were able to confirm the existence of those depleted uranium rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in the e-court system 5D319, please. This document hasn't got translation, so I will ask the witness to read second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please read the second paragraph, the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Infiltrated SAS members are close to military facilities and units. They are equipped with radio devices using high frequency for the purposes of communication and for -- to spot for the aeroplane and they carry light weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are SAS members?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the special units in the British Army, and they are used for special tasks, and they mostly operate in the depth of the territory of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. Could you please look at the heading here on this document. Is this a document that was issued by your administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As indicated here, the intelligence department at the command post issued this kind of documents. I believe this was obtained from the National Council and that its authenticity has been confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, my colleague Mr. Visnjic asked you about the negotiations in early June. You were a member of that delegation. I want to know whether you perhaps recall that the Pristina Corps units received and took care and provided support for the delegation that went to participate in those negotiations at Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Pristina Corps units received and accommodated our delegation, and they helped us get to the Djeneral Jankovic crossing. And once we crossed into Macedonia, that was the first day of the talks with the NATO representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps that en route to Djeneral Jankovic and Kacanicka Kresevo that an officer from 243 Mechanised Brigade was killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a tragic incident. As we were getting there, a captain from the communications unit in this brigade was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was this a terrorist act perpetrated by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it is undisputable that this was done by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on that occasion General Lazarevic went back to the command in order to prepare the units for the pullout from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the orders of the chief of the General Staff, General Lazarevic was to be a part of the delegation that went to participate in the talks. I don't know. He was not there. Probably with the agreement of the army commander and the chief of the General Staff, a decision was made for him to go back and to prepare the units for the pullout, because it was quite clear at that time that we would face this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now that we're talking about my client, General Lazarevic, did you in 2003 -- were you his superior officer in 2003?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the chief of the General Staff, and he was the deputy chief of General Staff for the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... System Exhibit Number 5D1363, please. [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we only have the Serbian or B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And, General, I would just like to ask you: Do you recognise this document? What sort of a document is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the usual form where army personnel got their evaluations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have page 2. Just a moment. While we still have page 1 on this document, this official evaluation, who is for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see here that it's the official evaluation of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you please look at this official evaluation. At the bottom of this document, is there your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first paragraph that begins with the words "in social context."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In social context, he is very much respected because of his great contribution to the defence of the country, his impeccable military bearing, and his -- the care that he takes of his people. He enjoys a great deal of respect from our citizens."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, taking care of the people, was this something that was very much a characteristic of General Lazarevic, as you indicated in this evaluation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time while I was his superior, this element of his personality came to the fore very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, what was the mark that General Lazarevic received?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see from this document, the evaluation was excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that from mid-1994 until April 1997 you were chief of the intelligence administration in the General Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the Chief of Staff during that time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, the chief of General Staff was Lieutenant General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to leave or why you left in April of 1997.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual practice in our army is to transfer people either laterally or to a higher position. I accepted this decision as a soldier, and I didn't really concern myself with the reasons why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So was it General Perisic's idea that you be transferred?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whose idea it was. Even if I were to ask, they'd tell me that it was the decision of the then-President of Serbia, Milosevic. But I didn't really investigate that, so I don't know whose idea it really was. But the decision, of course, was issued by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't harbour any resentment over that transfer, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. I went to take up a high position in the ministry, and even looking at the establishment hierarchy, it was a higher position. I tried to do the job given me by the minister with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you happily gave up that higher position to go back to your old job in January of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not about happily or unhappily. When I was returning to the duty of chief of the intelligence administration, that position was vacant at the time; whereas, the establishment rank that went with that duty was the same, lieutenant general -- lieutenant colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who had been serving in that position during late 1998 and before you came back in January 1999? Who did you replace?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1998, that position was occupied by Admiral Ladicorbic. But he was not chief of that administration. He was just occupying that position. And by law, in that year he had to be retired and the position remained vacant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I guess I didn't understand your answer about him occupying the position but not being the chief. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under our law, it is possible for a person to occupy not only his regular position but also to discharge duties at a higher level temporarily until that higher vacancy is filled, either by the person who acted in that position temporarily or a -- a different appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you came back in January 1999, Mr. Visnjic asked you about what was your assessment of the security situation. And in your answer yesterday, at page 16771, you said, . "Well, it contained quite a few positive elements,. Positive elements were based on the fact that in October 1998 an agreement had been reached between Holbrooke and Milosevic, and we sincerely believed that that marked the beginning of a peaceful political settlement for the conflict in Kosovo." And when you say "we" in that context, are you talking about the General Staff or the intelligence administration or all of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was prevailing sentiment in the General Staff among the colleagues from the collegium and the chief of the General Staff and in the administration which I headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I have a -- I have a question about how sincerely you could believe that that was possible, given the fact that the -- the VJ and, I would suggest, the MUP as well had violated the October agreements a number of times in various ways. First of all, the time you came back was right about the time Racak had happened; correct? You were aware of Racak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We all remember that tragic event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I remember, I think from the 21st of January collegium session, Exhibit P939 -- I can show you if I need to, but perhaps you'll remember. You spoke at that collegium, which may have been the first one you attended after you returned to your old job. And you mentioned that you had been told by a military attache that the VJ had been seen firing -- I can't remember if it was tank or artillery weapons in -- in support of that operation in Racak. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said yesterday, I had almost daily contacts with foreign military attaches in our country, and one of them shared this information with me. Of course, I understood that -- I took that very seriously, and that's why I reported it at the collegium of the General Staff. And if you look further through my statement, I insisted that the whole situation be cleared up and that we finally establish the truth of the matter, whether it was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Do you -- do you recall at a session of the VJ collegium on the 25th of February - that's Exhibit P941 - General Pantelic talked about new -- new army units going to Kosovo and Metohija. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that. I can't say it didn't happen that way, but I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: According to your understanding, that would have been a violation of the October agreement, would it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we know, the October agreement specified the number of units which should be in barracks and the number of units allowed to be on the ground, but it also specified that the KLA should not orchestrate provocations against the police and the army. At that time, however, there were some provocations already, and I remember that part of our units were at some level of readiness and some of these units did not go to Kosovo. They were deployed in areas outside Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the problem -- or you said it was specified that KLA wouldn't orchestrate provocations. KLA was not a signatory to the October agreements; right? That was only an agreement between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Holbrooke, between Serbia and NATO and the West; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll have to hear your answer out loud if -- once you've heard the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at Exhibit P935. General, this is the collegium session on the 11th of March, 1999. And I think I've got a hard copy here I'll give you that may make it easier to find. General, I think it's on page numbered 10 in the B/C/S -- or no, I'm sorry, page number 7. It's page 7 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. Sorry if I misled you. Do you find the portion where you're speaking?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, that's on page 6, page 6 but also page 4 and page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me find the exact spot here, General. I'm at page 6 of the English, and you're talking about the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke. At the top of page 7 in the English, there's a reference to the-- a Joint Command centre being formed, I guess, for the NATO forces in Skopje on the 4th of March. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija that existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean this Joint Command, the NATO one, or some other?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, not the NATO one but a -- a one for the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent of my knowledge at the time, I wasn't convinced there was a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to page 11 of the English. And General, I -- since I don't have the B/C/S in front of me, this is General Curcin speaking, near the bottom to have page in English -- bottom of the page in English. And you're -- I think that might be closer to page 9 for you. He's talking about 673 new troops deployed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and he's mentioning the 37th Motorised Brigade being relocated from the Raska Garrison to Kosovska Mitrovica [Realtime transcript read in error "Kosovo and Metohija"] and being re-subordinated to the Pristina Corps. He also mentions that the 21st Nis Corps had been relocated to the Urosevac sector and re-subordinated to the 243rd. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think in line 25 the reference was to Kosovska Mitrovica rather than Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to find that, General? I'm sorry, I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was in violation of the NATO agreement, wasn't it, bringing in those additional forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my job, I was not familiar with the details of those changes in our troop levels. As you see, this was within the remit of General Curcin, chief of the operations administration. But there was talk about personnel changes. Some people were leaving Kosovo; others were coming to take their place. And this is not about the re-subordination of the Nis Corps, to the brigade, because they are at different levels. The motorised brigade is on a tactical level. This was at the level of combat group, which is perhaps a reinforced company strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is you were at the collegium meeting where this was discussed, so you were aware at the time that these additional forces were being brought in to Kosovo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I attended that collegium meeting and I listened to these proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And did -- did General Ojdanic or anyone else at that collegium meeting express concern about this transfer or -- or increase of VJ forces in Kosovo and violating the October agreements? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that several times there was talk about the army having to adhere strictly to the October agreement, but I really can't recall every detail of this collegium meeting and everything that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to another topic. You testified yesterday about the -- the various sources of information you had in the intelligence administration. You've said that included communiques from state officials, from the major countries. You also used partially media reports. You used sources from military and civilian diplomacy and various operational sources. What do you mean by "operational sources"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you probably know that every intelligence service, in addition to public sources and the technology, has operative sources, that is, agents of different categories and different levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were any of those paid agents, paid by the army intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all sorts of agents. But the paid ones were easily in the minority, because we didn't have much money to pay them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your years in intelligence work, would you agree with me that -- that some of those sources from whom you got intelligence had to be viewed with a certain amount of scepticism or you would take their information, as I would say in my language, with a grain of salt. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think that applies to all intelligence services of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct. And one of the things that happens in the intelligence work is that the other side, if you will, is trying to mislead you sometimes -- sometimes deliberate misinformation is planted and passed on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that, too, is part of the doctrine of certain armies and certain intelligence services, that so-called strategic deceiving can be used to mislead the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It works both ways; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on the capacities of a particular service for this subtle kind of work, because it is very subtle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I agree, it is subtle. And sometimes misinformation or disinformation can come to you from an otherwise reliable agent who has been fed that information and unknowingly passes it along believing it to be correct. That happens, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in theory and in practice, that can happen, because as you know, there are so-called double agents, that is, agents who work for one service, for another, and maybe even a third one. And they can also serve as channels for passing on that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to ask you about another collegium meeting. This one was on the 25th of February. And there was a discussion about the -- the Paris talks. This was after Rambouillet and before Paris. And I think you raised the issue - tell me if you recall - you raised the possibility that it should be suggested that military, people from the army or from the collegium or the General Staff, should be considered for participating in those talk, because of the expertise you could bring to military issues. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that was my idea, my idea shared by some other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that General Ojdanic supported that idea, and you said: "As far as I can remember, he presented it to the state authorities." Do you recall any details about what you know about General Ojdanic presenting it to the state authorities? Who did he present it to? When? Where? And what was the reaction? Anything further you can tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really can't say any more about that, because I know no more. General Ojdanic did not inform us to whom he passed on these proposals, who accepted them or who rejected them. The fact is that there were no members of the army on that delegation, and it follows therefore that the idea was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm -- I apologise, General, I have to go back to one thing before I forget. I asked you about Joint Command. I think at your -- at the VJ collegium session on the 21st of January, where there was some discussion about Racak, General Ojdanic mentioned the Joint Command "down there," which seemed to be a reference to Kosovo. Do you recall him mentioning that in that January 21st collegium session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can hardly remember every word uttered by every person at a collegium meeting. I cannot really say I remember he mentioned that Joint Command in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was as a -- as a military professional, would that term contain some significance for you? "Joint Command" is sort of a special term, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a special term. A command in itself is an institution within the structure of every army. There are commands, units and institutions. A command is established by a regulation. And as far as I know, no regulation pertaining to that Joint Command existed. The structure of a command should be strictly regulated. And as far as I know, what some people refer to as "Joint Command" did not have a structure that would be appropriate to a command. And specifically I can confidently confirm that there was no intelligence organ there, and it's hardly believable that on the eve of a war there could be a command without an intelligence component. Quite certainly I never submitted a single piece of information to that command, nor did I ever receive any information or anything else from that command. So I believe it was not a command in the traditional sense. It could have been perhaps a group for the coordination of certain activities in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me show you something specific from that meeting. This is Exhibit P939. If we could go to page 12 of the English. And I think it's at page 10 of the -- the Serbian. General, perhaps I can hard you a hard copy of this one. If you'll give me back that old one, I'll give you this new one. And I know at the bottom it may say "24 December 1998," but I will tell you that I think that's just a -- an artifact from an earlier computer-generated version of other minutes. And this is for the 21st of January. And do you find page 10? I think you're speaking on page 11, but on page 10 about two-thirds of the way down, that is General Ojdanic speaking. And he is saying -- it's -- the sentence starts out: "There's yet another option." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's an option: "The Joint Command down there whereby the President orders me, and I have to know it immediately." And it says: "By order of the President of the FRY, do the seriousness of the situation, such-and-such forces and assets of some of the Pristina Corps units shall be engaged and everything is fine and there's no problem." Now, he seems to be discussing how things might work better in the future so he would be informed about what was happening, because in this meeting there's a discussion about Racak and the uncertainty that the collegium and General Ojdanic feel about not knowing exactly what happened down there and whether any of the VJ elements were involved. That -- that's correct? That was the gist of the meeting, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way, that it was the gist. But from the passage you read, if we are interpreting this correctly, General Ojdanic was speaking hypothetically, that there is an option to form a Joint Command there and it could have been formed perhaps. But as far as I know, it wasn't. We had one Joint Command in the south of Central Serbia when in 2000 and 2001 we had a crisis there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Are you saying you read that to say that the Joint Command didn't yet exist and he's proposing that it be formed? I read that -- it sounds like there is a Joint Command in existence and what he's proposing is that the President tell him, General Ojdanic, what's going to be done, inform him. Isn't that what it means?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated, but way I read it, there is this option of forming a Joint Command, rather than the Joint Command existing already. In Serbian, it says: "There is or there exists another option. To have a Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read that B/C/S paragraph word for word, or is that what you just did?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There is another option. There's the option of a Joint Command down there." And then the President gives me an order and I have to know it immediately. And then it says: "On the orders of the FRY President, due to the gravity of the situation, part of the units of the Pristina Corps join in with such-and-such forces and such-and-such assets and then the whole thing is okay and there are no problems." Let me show you an exhibit, then, from -- from April of 1999. This is P1487. I want to suggest to you, General, that the Joint Command did exist in January 1999 and that it also existed in April of 1999. Can you see this one? This is a document dated the 17th of April, 1999 from the Supreme Command Staff, staff operations department, operations administration, signed by General Ojdanic. We may have to scroll down to the bottom of the B/C/S page so you can see that. Do you agree with me so far?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is obvious from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go back to page 1 of the English for me, you'll see that there is a reference. It says: "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, strictly confidential number 455-148 of 15 April 1999." And then there are some -- some suggestions from General Ojdanic. Would you agree with me, General, that that seems to indicate that there is a body in existence called the Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command and that they've issued some sort of order to the 3rd Army command? Isn't that a reasonable reading of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that's a formal reading of this document. In my view, it would be good to look at the substance of what is written, and this line where it says: "Reference: Order of the Joint Command," number such-and-such. I think it would be good to have a look at this document, this order of the Joint Command, and to analyse that document in detail. And then we could reach a conclusion as to whether that was really an order and whether it was really a Joint Command. And what is written here, of course, is indisputable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can do that for you in a minute, General. But are you telling me -- you worked in intelligence. You're a smart guy. I see from your CV that you speak, I don't know, six, seven, eight languages. You don't -- you can't take from this that there must be a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija that's in existence? Isn't that a rational conclusion that you would make in analysing a document like this, a guy who works in military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that is an irrational conclusion. I was just trying to suggest that we should look at it in depth, not only a formal reading but a detailed analysis and then and see what's behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I should indicate that Exhibit P1878, which I think is the Joint Command order referred to here, was not something I included on my list of things I was going to cross-examine about. But in light of the answer I got, I would ask permission to use that right now for my next couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecution would allow me to introduce a document of my own with some future witness, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean any document any time, Mr. Visnjic? Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are authorised to use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put Exhibit P1878 on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before we go, General, you see that was number 455-148 is the Joint Command Order number referred to. Do you see that? Now, hopefully we'll have it for you in a minute, and we'll see a document dated the 15th of April, 1999. And it should have that same number, 455-148. I think you've got it in B/C/S now. If we could split the screen so I can see the English. I don't have my copy in front of me. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you -- could you read the -- the title of that document. What -- what's it about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Strictly confidential number 455-148."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14th April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's an order to break up and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Rogovo sector; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you go to the last page of this document in both English and Serbian. And then I'll have one more question, I think, and then we'll take a break, General. And we see it doesn't have a signature. There's just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, please. If the Prosecutor is introducing a document that hasn't been announced, can he introduce it in its entirety. Could General Krga first see page 2 and then page 3. Let him read the first part, the next page, and then the third page, to whom this order is issued. That's very important. Because I, too, have an interest in the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what do you say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think for my present purposes it's not necessary to do that. It can be address on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. So please continue the way you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see there's a typewritten name: "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" on the last page. No signature; correct? You'll see that immediately above that, if -- if I can go back one page in the English. It says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command all forces from the Pristina sector during the conduct of combat operations." So would you agree with me this appears to be an order for the conducting of combat operations, a joint operation between VJ and MUP forces? Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Shall we hear the explanation of "yes and no" before we take the break, Your Honour? Please go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, again, we read this document formally, then that's the conclusion you could draw. However, if we look at para 2 of the document, where under our instructions and the work of commands and staffs an assignment is given to the units subordinated to that command, then we see that only the Pristina Corps is concerned, not units of the Ministry of the Interior. Therefore, this looks to me like an order of the commander of the Pristina Corps. And the fact that it is not signed runs counter to all our rules on the drafting of documents titled "Orders." Every order must be signed and it must be known who takes responsibility for issuing that order, which is in keeping with the principle of the unity of command in our army and in every other army. And as counsel feel I mentioned the fact that assignments are given to units indicates that -- or rather, we see that assignments are given only to the units of the Pristina Corps, not the MUP, which means that this Joint Command was not really superior to the MUP units, and we can reach the conclusion that this order applies only to the Pristina Corps. Why this was named "Joint Command," I really can't say. It could be perhaps a good idea to check the authenticity of these documents and whether they are really original in terms of the heading and the unsigned signature line, "Joint Command," because every other indicator points that it is an order of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Again it is a transcript. It says 40 -- page 40, line 6, "the unity of command." I believe the witness said "the singleness of command, in keeping with the principle of singleness of command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not come to the same thing? Is the expression of "unity of command" not used regularly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness said "singleness," keeping with the principle of singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I must make some objection, and I'll do it as quickly as I can. I think Mr. Hannis is being decidedly unfair with regard to this matter. First of all, he says to the witness when talking about the first document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just -- just hold on a second. We're going to have a break, Mr. Krga, just now, and we'll be resuming in 20 minutes, so could you again leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He first suggests to the witness when he has the witness looking at P1487 that -- says to the witness, "Doesn't this appear to be some kind of an order to the 3rd Army," which he knows it's not because he's totally familiar with 4 -- 545-148. He was trying to get the witness to accept something that he knew was not the case. Secondly, he says to the witness to him: "In order to understand, this an analysis of the document needs to be done." He says to the witness then: "I can do that in a minute, General." And then when Mr. Fila suggests that the witness should be permitted to do that, if he told him he could do, Mr. Hannis says, "No, I only want him to look at the first page and the last page," I don't really want him to see what the order says, which he already told he would give him a chance to analyse. And what he's trying to do is to create a false representation of what this is. This is a order that deals only with Pristina Corps, VJ people and it's not even a valid order in my view, and it has nothing to do with Joint Command or MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are all matters that can be dealt with in any submissions you have to make in due course, and it may be that -- that you ought to have the opportunity to ask the witness further questions. But no doubt Mr. Visnjic has the line you're referring to in mind. We have to bear in mind the possibility, of course, Mr. Ackerman, that these documents are designed to be confusing and misleading. These are matters for us to resolve eventually in -- in this case. And if the Prosecution wants to go about cross-examination in a particular way which doesn't prevent re-examination to clarify points, then it's difficult for us to find a basis for interfering. So we will allow Mr. Hannis to proceed the way he has chosen to proceed so far, and we'll do that again at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I just say one more thing for the record, Your Honour? Although the -- the right to cross-examination or redirect exists, I don't think I'm permitted, and I don't think any lawyer in this case should be permitted to attempt to mislead a witness to try to get an answer that might be helpful to his case. I think you have to be honest with the witness about what the document is. And when you're not doing that, when you're intentionally misleading, I think you are violating all of the Rules, and that's what's going on here and I object very strongly here. I won't do it and I have more pride than that, and I think it's unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I can't allow that to go unanswered. What do you say about the allegation that you're deliberately misleading the witness and the Court, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's utterly false, Your Honour. I may have misspoken when referring to the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, but I'm not intentionally misleading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll give a decision on this point when we return after the break. And that will now be at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the matter raised immediately before we left the courtroom, we do not consider that Mr. Hannis has deliberately misled the witness in any way. Indeed, a simple reference to the witness's answers makes it clear that he understood clearly what he was being asked and was able to deal with the questions. In addition, there remains the right to re-examine on any matter on which it's necessary to clarify anything that needs further expansion. So we will proceed. If there are any further questions on the document, then we consider it appropriate for Mr. Hannis to follow the line he's been following so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to say for the record that I accept Mr. Hannis' suggestion that at page 36, lines 11 through 14, when he mentioned an order to the 3rd Army, that he misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks very much, Mr. Ackerman. We assumed that would be the position, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I just wanted to clear something up, because there was some concern that I -- I might have misled you about this document P1878. I -- I think I had referred to the order as being directed to the 3rd Army, and I understand really the Pristina Corps. And I gather you understood that from -- from your answers. Is that fair? You have to answer out loud. I saw you nod your head, but we need an answer on the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the -- but for me the point I was trying to make, it appears that somebody called some organ -- some organ or some body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija was issuing combat orders to elements of the VJ and in particular the Pristina Corps. And in the earlier exhibit P1487, which are the suggestions from General Ojdanic, the highest uniformed officer in the VJ, it -- it seems to me that General Ojdanic is giving some deference to this body called the Joint Command, because he's not overriding their order. He's making suggestions. Do you have any comment on that as a professional career soldier?, in terms of chain of command and singleness of command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used an imprecise expression, Supreme Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Yes, it's "Joint Command" you said. But as far as I know, General Ojdanic and my colleagues, we always endeavoured to keep the chain of command perfectly clear and simple and for there to be no doubt about it. Therefore, the existence of a Joint Command, as I said, during those dramatic events was not something I was aware of. Had such a command existed, I would have had to be aware of it. An analysis of the documents which are registered as emanating from that Joint Command, it transpires that that was the command of the Pristina Corps rather than some sort of Joint Command. Tasks are issued only to units of the Pristina Corps, and there's nothing joint about that. As far as I know, there was one document signed by General Lazarevic. There is no doubt that General Lazarevic was the commander of the Pristina Corps. He could not have simultaneously been the commander of the Pristina Corps and the commander of some Joint Command which is said to have existed. Therefore, I assume, as I wasn't down there and I wasn't part of the structures mentioned, I can only assume that there existed some sort of coordinating body which someone through inertia or whatever labeled a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your position -- is it your position that there was a body called the Joint Command but it -- you -- you maintained it had no authority to command; rather, it was only a coordinating body? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there were several people from the political structures who coordinated life and work on Kosovo and Metohija -- in Kosovo and Metohija, and probably there was some kind of cooperation with the army and the MUP and they coordinated and made proposals. But I'm certain they had no right to issue executive orders to those units. That would have had to be done within the established chain of command, which was based on the law and the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, look at paragraph number 13 of the document on the screen. Now, what -- what -- how does the second sentence there fit with what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the second sentence is not quite in line with what I said, but the first sentence goes to confirm it, because as you can see, it says "joint action with MUP forces will be organised." Had there been a Joint Command, the words "joint action" would not have been mentioned but tasks would have been issued to the MUP, just as they were issued to the brigades of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it possible some body responsible for coordinating the activities of these forces passed their orders through the regular chain of command so that this document might be matched by a similar document through the normal chain of MUP command? In other words, this was an executive order based on a -- an order sent by a Joint Command to both forces; that's both the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is quite logical, and I understand it. But I wish to suggest once more that the authenticity of this document be established or that the authors of the document be asked about it. I am saying what I know and basing my answer on the principles of military organisation and the system of command. This runs counter to the prescribed system of command. Had somebody -- well, I can neither confirm nor deny that somebody drafted this document. But how it came about, I really couldn't say. I can't know, because I wasn't there, I didn't participate in those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My impression is that what you're really saying is that this document can't be genuine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying it's not. But by your leave, I am suggesting that the authenticity be verified, because it seems a bit unusual, odd in view of its heading and signature, of the fact that you can't see who it was addressed to. Documents of this kind, documents such as orders, in almost all of our commands contain these elements. I don't believe that a command complying with the rules would make such omissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Well, I tell you that that particular document was received from your government and it was located in the VJ archives. Would that change your position about whether it's authentic or not, if it comes from the archives?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it comes from the archives, which I believe you -- you're -- I believe what you say, then it must be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you two additional documents to try and further unravel the -- the mystery about this. First of all, I want to show you P1966. Now, I'll hand you a hard copy, General. And I'll give you the next one too as well, P1967. The first one, General, P1966, is from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija on the 22nd of March, 1999, and it's an order to route and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Malo Kosovo area. Now, if you want to take a minute to look through it. Could you do so and tell me if that appears to be in the general form -- or consistent with the ordinary form of a combat order issued by the VJ. In 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part the contents of this document are in line with this kind of document, as written in the Yugoslav Army at the time. I wish to point out, however, a few features which I feel are important in order to establish the nature of this document. First of all, in paragraph 2, the tasks of the Pristina Corps. If there had been a Joint Command, a Joint Command would not make sense unless there are joint forces it is in command of. And then in paragraph 2 it should have said "task for the joint forces." For example, Pristina Corps and the MUP units' task. According to our rules, paragraph 2 always contains that element. An overall task is assigned to the unit that the command is superior to, the command that issued the document. In point 5 -- under heading 5, where tasks for the units are mentioned, details are provided concerning what is contained in headings 2 and 4. And each unit that that command is in command of is assigned a task. And as we can see, the only units mentioned here were part of the Pristina Corps or were re-subordinated to it. There are no other units mentioned here. So there's nothing joint here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me -- let me --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only units of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there and ask you a question. Item 5.2, "Tasks for units." And this one's for the 125th Motorised Brigade, combat group 4, it appears. Its task is: "In coordination with PJP," right? So that's a joint task. That has MUP units involved; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. It does contemplate that task being carried out in coordination with a MUP unit to do the same job; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the usual practice in our army and other armies as well. One assigns a task to one's unit, and also mention is made of the fact that another unit under another command might participate. These special units of the police, had they been under this command, then under heading 5.4, a precise task would have been assigned to them as well. Special units of the police, acting jointly with the 125th would have been given such a task. That would have been the normal practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it could have been done the way Judge Bonomy suggested before the break, couldn't it? That there would have been in essence a mirror order going through the MUP chain of command for that PJP company to work in coordination with the 125th Motorised Brigade in carrying out the attack along that axis. Correct? You allow for that possibility, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably there was a command that was the superior command of the PJP which gave them such a task; otherwise, this would make no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is issued only by the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you back to item 2, the Pristina Corps task. It says: "The Pristina Corps, with reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population shall conduct an attack in the area." What was the armed non-Siptar population that was working in coordination with the Pristina Corps in carrying out this combat activity? Do you know who that was or what that was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer with precision what this refers to. Perhaps some structures of the civil defence and civilian protection. I assume you're aware of the fact that for a long time we had the doctrine of All People's Defence, where the idea of the armed population existed, and this might have been left -- been left behind due to inertia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Or it could have been because the non-Siptar population in Kosovo was provided arms by the army. You were at a meeting of the collegium on the 2nd of February, 1999, weren't you? Well, I know you were, because you spoke at that collegium session. Right? And we'll come to that in a minute. But the point I want to make was at that meeting General Samardzic advised the collegium and General Ojdanic about the thousands of non-Siptars who had been provided with weapons in Kosovo. Do you recall that being discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, evidently that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if you'll go back to the first page. I just want you to see this order is number 455-56. Will you bear that number in mind for a moment. Do you see that? Okay. And the last page of that document, again, has similar language to what we saw before. It says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command and direct all forces during combat operations from the Pristina area." That's what it says; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you look at the next document. It's P1967, also dated the 22nd of March. And you'll see the number on that order is 455-56/1. We've heard other evidence that that numbering would indicate that this is a document that relates to the one you just looked at. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You have to answer aloud. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this one is entitled "Amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP in breaking up and destroying the Siptar terrorists in the area of Malo Kosovo." And if you'll go to the last page, you'll see this one has a signature and a stamp and delivery information. And based on what you told Mr. Cepic before, I assume you recognise that as the signature of General Lazarevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So maybe I'm making an overly formal reading here, but this seems like General Lazarevic is -- is recognising the authority of the Joint Command, whatever or whoever that is, and he's making an amendment to their decision. Isn't that what this document is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could -- could say that this is the case and that it isn't the case. In essence, the two documents have the same character. As you can see, the reference number for the two documents, you can see it here, but to me this indicates that all this had to do with the Pristina Corps command. And let me repeat once again, if anything joint existed here, I can't know that for certain but perhaps some police units had been re-subordinated to the Pristina Corps and then by dint of that this became joint. But this is not apparent from the document. Had -- had this been the case, those units would be assigned specific tasks. I've already said this, but let me repeat. And you probably agree with me that General Lazarevic could not have been at the same time the commander of the Pristina Corps, which was undoubted - he was the commander of that corps - and the commander of another command, a Joint Command or whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do agree with you about that, because otherwise why would he be issuing an amendment signed and stamped by him to an order that he had written without his signature. That doesn't make sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could make sense if in the meantime some new elements occurred requiring an amendment to be drafted specifying the new elements and regulating their implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but I -- I guess what I'm saying is I understood part of your -- one of your earlier answers to be suggesting that perhaps General Lazarevic was the one who wrote the original order, 455-56, that is, P1966.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But that doesn't make sense. Why isn't his signature and stamp on that one? These are both done the same day.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and that's why I'm confused myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But one possible explanation, one reasonable explanation is that the Joint Command was some separate body called the Joint Command - and maybe for your purposes a coordinating body - but it is the body that generated this order, 455-56.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the witness is now asked to speculate. He has already indicated what he knows, and now he's just being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What's being asked is not a matter of speculation for a man who has recently been the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and was directly involved in these events at the time. So we repel that objection. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just give you a more specific answer to your question. The order as some kind of a basic document was drafted by one structure, one command, and the amendment to the decision by another command. This could not have happened under our rules. If one command issued or drafted one order, any amendments to the decision pursuant to that order could only have been drafted by the same command. The subordinate command, command subordinate to the one that drafted the initial order, could have then drafted its own order specifying the tasks for the units under its command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I -- I certainly didn't follow your -- your point about it being illogical for a second one to be amending another order made by General Lazarevic. Just looking at the terms of -- of the first one, why could it not be an implementation order? That's P1966 -- that was subsequently amended by P1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess if Your Honour views 1966 as not being a implementation order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what's the difference between the two of them in form?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the signature and the seal and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apart from that. Just looking at the form of the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I -- I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- but to me both written on the same day, why is one signed and stamped and the other one not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I dare say there's a number of possible explanations for that, including whether you have the original of both or not. And how many copies were kept and how they were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
