utterances.text: Okay. I take it -- I take that point, Your Honour. And -- well, that's something I have to save for submissions. I -- I shouldn't make that comment in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And 1967, General, does not contain any modification to the provision in 1966, which says that the Joint Command shall command all the combat operations, all the forces during combat operations; right? That's unchanged in the amendment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that 1967 does not contain the repeated provision that the Joint Command shall be in command and control of all the forces during the combat operations. It is indicated here that the command post shall be established in the village of Lausa, the command post of that command that made this amendment to the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move now to another topic. You told Mr. Visnjic that you had some experiences from the reactions to the Racak incident and the fact that your forces were blamed for that and you were concerned that something like that would occur again, that there'd be another incident that could be used as a pretext for the use of NATO forces. And -- and I think this is the time period in February and March before the war that you were talking about. Now, weren't you also worried about real incidents where your forces might have attacked without provocation and -- and not in response to an initial attack by the KLA? Wasn't that something that the collegium was concerned about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the position that I had, I focused my attention on the forces in the region and the KLA. And as for the activities of our forces, this was monitored by other elements in the General Staff, so that perhaps I was duty-bound to do so, but I cannot claim now that I knew about every single movement our units carried out on the ground. I was concerned that our activities might perhaps cause a negative response on the part of NATO that would be detrimental to our security and defence. And every time I obtained such information, I would point out that this should be prevented, this should be put under control, and that we should not be the ones who would be supplying any kind of pretext for the conflict to escalate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that wasn't just your concern; that was a concern shared by others on the General Staff, and in particular one person who voiced that concern was General Dimitrijevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Dimitrijevic was a colleague of mine. He was the chief of the security administration. There were some other people too. But I often agreed with him on this issue, but there were some dissenting opinions that were based on perhaps different information that our two services had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me hand you a hard copy of the next exhibit I want to ask you about. This is Exhibit P938. This is a collegium session from the 18th of March, and I'm looking at page 11 in the English. And the B/C/S, I think it's page number 9 for you, General. In e-court, it's actually page 10 in the B/C/S. And this is General Dimitrijevic talking. It's fairly in the middle of a very long conversation. But if you can find it, he's talking about -- I think I've highlighted it or marked it with a marker. It says: "With respect to that too, the theory that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping-up operations of the territory are exceptionally widespread. Every morning I read very carefully and in great detail the Pristina Corps combat reports, and there was not a single case where we were conducting something. Instead, they are always attacking us and we return fire." He goes on to say: "I propose that we should discuss that here at the General Staff level, at least. Even if not everyone should know everything, I think that you" -- and I think in this context he's referring to General Ojdanic -- "I think that you more than anyone should know the real truth, because you're the personalisation of the whole institution. Something is not right here." And before I ask the question, can I ask you to go to one more comment by Dimitrijevic on that, and it's at page 21 of the English. And for you, General, I think that will be page 22 in your hard copy and page 23 in the B/C/S e-court. And he says: "There have been 16 attacks on our army units in one week. Did a single one of those operations occur while we were carrying out a previously planned operation and was not an attack? I would like someone to tell me. I contend that the yesterday's two were conducted by us and that we were not attacked. In other words, we did not launch an operation following an attack on one of our units by terrorists but, instead, as they say, a mopping-up of the terrain operation had been launched. Hence, it was presumably supported by the MUP." Do you recall that being discussed and that concern raised in this meeting of 18th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the interpreters are commenting. This is page 19 in the B/C/S for the witness to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have the text. I received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have misspoke the number, but we highlighted the provision in the witness's copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall my question, or do I need to repeat it? Do you recall this being -- this concern being raised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was raised in the manner that you just presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what the outcome of the discussion was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall with great certainty, but I do know that General Ojdanic always insisted that everything that was going on in that area should be kept under control so that, on the one hand, we would not be the ones to blame for the incidents, and, on the other hand, that we should not be surprised, that our forces should not be targeted by the KLA, should not suffer casualties because of that. Now, as to what specifically was done after this collegium meeting, whether any orders were issued to the units of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, I really couldn't now tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me then follow up by showing you another exhibit. This is P1999. I'll hand you a hard copy, General. This is dated the 18th of March, 1999, the same day as that collegium session we were just looking at. This is from the 549th Motorised Brigade, Commander General -- or Colonel -- then Colonel Delic. And he's reporting about an action that was carried out on the 17th of March pursuant to an order the Pristina Corps command that had been issued on the 16th of March. And it's an operation in the vicinity of the Kabas village. You'll see under item number 1 that they estimated the strength of the terrorists in that location to be between 30 and 35 men. And if you'll go down one, two, three paragraphs, it says - and it's the next page in English, page 2 - "During the operation, the terrorists did not drop their weapons or combat equipment until the last moment. When they changed into civilian clothes and attempted to break through along a certain axis, where they came across our units in the line of the blockade." And the estimated losses were 11 terrorists killed, no one was captured. Let me ask you a question about that: Does that mean the terrorists who had switched into civilian clothes and ran into the blockade, were killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult for me to comment on it, because this is the first time that I see this document. And we at the Supreme Command Staff did not receive reports or documents from tactical units. As you can see, this report was submitted to the Pristina Corps command. Now, we can form various assumptions as to what actually happened there, but those who took part in it know that for sure and they can be reliable witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. You'll see below that the -- the -- in item number 2: "The forces involved, about 600 VJ personnel and about 350 policemen. So some 950 for the 30 to 35 terrorists that were in the village. And the equipment used: Six tanks, a couple Howitzers, et cetera. You were aware at that time there were lots of concerns raised in the International Community about excessive force being used in these operations; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was present in the official reactions in the media, the issue of excessive use of force. Although, no doctrine and no rules specify what it means, the balance of power that is necessary for the conclusion that there was excessive use of force. During NATO airstrikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I think we could talk about excessive use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Answer to my question. And you'll see on the last page where Colonel Delic signs, the -- the amount and types of ammunition used in that operation; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and the point I wanted to make was this -- this document describes an offensive operation by the VJ in coordination with the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's the thing that Dimitrijevic was expressing concerns about, that they were getting reports that in all instance the VJ had been attacked and they were just responding. But this appears to be an action that is initiated by the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't necessarily follow that the army launched -- initiated this action, because it would not be proper to look at army actions in an isolated way, to look at just one day, one -- because we don't know what the KLA forces had done the day before. Perhaps they had attacked the army units, inflicted casualties; perhaps they had attacked the population, and then a decision was possibly made to target that group, to attack it. So I can't really tell you what actually happened. Perhaps this should be analysed in greater detail. But theoretically and in practical terms it is possible. It is possible that these forces and the units of the 249th Brigade had engaged in combat previously, and this may be just the final act, this clash that is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So how far back in time do we go before we can say that it's an attack and not a response to a prior attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time of the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija, whenever those incidents occurred, the question that was always asked was: What is action and what is reaction to the action? As you know, there were many such incidents, and it is impossible to give you a -- a brief answer to -- to tell you which side engaged in more actions, as opposed to reactions. But I am sure of one thing: Our units had their task, and they had their interest in not having the conflict to escalate any further, because any escalation was counter to the interests of the country, the army and the country in general, because we knew the possible consequences, strategically speaking for the defence of the country, so that I'm quite certain that my colleagues on the ground wanted to have no conflicts, but those conflicts or clashes occurred. This was more or less quite well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suggest another possibility to you, General, and that's the forces on the ground who were actually living there in Kosovo and seeing their comrades injured and killed did want to attack and wanted to attack first, rather than waiting for the next time that they were ambushed by the KLA. Isn't that a reasonable possibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the tactical level, on the ground such actions are a possibility. Definitely. And it's quite logical, after all, from the point of view of legally speaking, they are justified. Because you don't want your units to sustain any more casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I can see where there would be a difference of perspective from the private or the sergeant on the ground in Kosovo who's living with that from day to day. He may not share the concern of the VJ collegium or the political leadership at the highest level about, We're being watched by the International Community and we don't want to start any incidents, so we can only respond when attacked. That makes sense. That's how it works in real life, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a whole spectrum of the levels of command and situations that people found themselves in, situations where their soldiers, their close relatives, friends were being -- were getting killed, and emotions were involved. Quite apart from the tasks and rules and regulations that came from the level of the Supreme Command, the 3rd Army command, and the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And along that chain of command from the private up to General Ojdanic, I suggest to you that it's also a reasonable possibility that someone in between those two extremes might find it useful to carry out attacks and not report it up. Isn't that a possibility, considering all the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At various levels of command, commanders, "komandiri" and "komandanti" had the right to respond once they established that they were either under attack or that an attack was imminent. At that tactical level, it was difficult to establish who provoked in some way an attack. But I do know that the commanders at all levels always reported all that up the chain of command. So it is difficult to assume that if a platoon or if a company comes under attack and then you have to wait for the General Staff to give you their approval to defend themselves, to respond. Under the military rules, they were duty-bound to defend their unit against the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. And -- and that makes sense. But the operation that we saw in Exhibit P1999 seemed to be something that was put together with some thought and organisation, involving 600 VJ members and some 350 MUP, tanks, Howitzers, et cetera. That's not just an immediate response to an immediate attack. With 950 on one side and 30 KLA on the other. Right? This is -- this is an offensive operation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can't know what preceded these events and what gave rise to this response on the part of the command of the 249th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'll move on. I understand your point. You -- you mentioned it before. Now I want to ask you about -- you talked about a meeting you had on the 12th of March with US military attache Colonel Pemberton, where you told us you proposed that there be an exchange of officers between NATO and the VJ. But I'm asking you: Wasn't it true that General Clark had proposed to General Ojdanic that Ojdanic come to the NATO headquarter, and that had been the week before or the same week as your meeting on the 12th of March. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right on both counts. General Clark invited General Ojdanic to come to Brussels with six of his men to clear up some of the issues that were topical at the time. It's correct that I suggested to the US military attache to have an exchange of officers, to send ours to Brussels and to receive their officers in Belgrade, and I wanted the misunderstandings that were already common at the time to be cleared up as efficiently and as quickly as possible, and we already had complaints from certain western countries that the October agreement was being violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and the point I -- I wanted to make was that General Clark had made that initiative to General Ojdanic but he had not attended. He apparently had other engagements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why General Ojdanic did not go to that meeting. I know that he had a good opinion of that initiative. I'm not sure whether he had gone to the President to discuss it and what transpired there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some of the documents that were shown to you. And this concerns the -- the meetings -- the various kinds of meetings and briefings that were held with General Ojdanic in the -- between the start of the war, the 24th of March, to the end of it in June. Now, we have in evidence the -- the handwritten notes that were kept of the evening briefings that I think initially started out at 8.00 or 8.30 at night and then later on they start at 6.00 at night. We've got those records. And we understand from the testimony of yourself and other witnesses that there were also morning meetings. Who participated in those morning meetings? Was that the collegium? Was that the Supreme Command Staff? Who -- who were the participants in the morning meetings? And what were they called?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning meetings were not as regular as the evening ones. In fact, they were rather rare. And they were not attended by the entire composition, the 15 or 18 people that attended the evening briefings. However, for purposes of that morning meeting, we provided a short brief about the events of the previous night from the evening meeting until the early morning hours, and we made it available to the chief of the General Staff. But morning meetings were held only when strictly necessary to discuss a certain issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And who -- who determined when those meetings were necessary? Who scheduled them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings were convened in one of two ways: Most often the chief of the General Staff would invite those persons he thought necessary, but we members of the General Staff could also initiate a meeting at the office of the chief of the General Staff or perhaps invite other persons to clear up a certain issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone keep minutes of these morning meetings? And if so, who was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think minutes were kept. They were not held very formally, these morning meetings. It was a meeting where a member of the collegium would write down the outcome of the discussion, the one who raised the issue in the first place, and would inform the chief of the General Staff eventually. But there were no regular minutes kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've seen two different kinds of documents from you. We -- we've seen some things called intelligence reports, which seem to be the more formal documents you prepared. They're usually more detailed. They have more analysis. Those usually have your signature and a stamp on them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We at the intelligence administration had several types of documents, and one of them is the one you mentioned. It was a daily brief that comprised a number of elements and was intended to provide a comprehensive view of the current situation and perhaps included some proposals and suggestions. Some documents concentrated on one issue alone, while other documents dealt with everything that was discussed at briefings. So it was not a -- a definitively determined format. I would take up an issue discussed at a briefing, would include some things that were discussed, were reported, and would exclude some elements which in the meantime I found out to be incorrect or irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have a look at Exhibit 3D934. And these other documents that I've seen referred to as intelligence briefings, and they usually have a number such as 2/99 or 12/99, are these the daily briefings you're talking about? And when -- when were these used? Are these your talking notes or is this a written submission you make to General Ojdanic? How are these used?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we see on the screen now, 43/99, is the draft, my own personal reminder for my presentation at the evening collegium meeting at the office of the chief of General Staff. It was not submitted as such to the chief of General Staff. Rather, many elements from this, plus some additional ones, were presented as a brief with a different number to the chief of General Staff and other colleagues from the General Staff and some other users.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So these were prepared by yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents were prepared as indicated below. A group of people, the intelligence section of the Supreme Command Staff. This group of people was with me at the command staff. They worked in shifts and they entered these elements as they received information. And, of course, I reviewed it all at the end and I am the only one who has responsibility for everything that is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, so is the -- the Serbian that we see on the screen in the left, is this the original format in which they were prepared back in 1999? This is the original document that was created then? Or -- or were they handwritten and then typed up later? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. In that room of the intelligence section, they were handwritten -- or rather, they were typed up on a PC. Elements were entered in the course of the have day -- of the day as information -- relevant information came in and as we analysed it to see if it's relevant or not, accurate or not. And then we printed out this paper so that I could review it before going to the briefing. I revised it, deleted something, added something. After that, this document was no longer edited. As you see, it hasn't been entered into any register. It was not submitted to anyone. It just served as a draft for one-time use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And where were these kept, then, from the time they were created in 1999 until today? Because most of these documents that we see related to the army have -- have signatures and seals and stamps and all kinds of things. Do you understand my question? Where do these come from? Where were they kept since 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1999 onwards, these documents were kept at the archives of the intelligence administration. And as you can see, they are quite original. Nothing was amended, added, modified. They were not destroyed. And, of course, if we had known then that we would be reading them one day in The Hague, maybe the contents would look different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page of this document. You'll see item number 14, which appears to be something about an exercise that's part of the Partnership for Peace has been stricken through. Do you know when that was done?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already said that when I received a document of this kind, I would look at it before my presentation to the collegium and I would make some changes. I believed that this part was not important and I crossed it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that from 1999 onwards these documents were kept at the archives of the intelligence administration. Is that a separate archive from where all the rest of the army documents are kept?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every institution in our country, every administration, every sector has a part of its archives that it keeps on its own premises for a while. Once a certain time has expired and these documents are no longer topical or important or relevant, they are handed over to the central archives. This particular document doesn't even deserve to be handed over to the central archives because it was a draft, not an approved document. And it could have been kept at the intelligence administration for a while and it could even have been destroyed with minutes of the destruction drawn up. However, this one has survived and you can see what transpired there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess my question, though, it's just a -- just a matter of chain of custody of evidence. I can't tell by looking at this document -- I mean, I understand what you're saying, but how can we tell by looking at this document that it wasn't prepared last week or last year, as opposed to 1999? There's no signature. There's no stamp. There's no record from the archives showing when it came in and when it went out. You understand my question? Can you -- can you tell us how we can have confidence that this is the original as it was prepared back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assert with complete certainty that it's that original, because I know that no documents were doctored at the intelligence administration and that these documents were probably provided maybe at the request of the National Council for cooperation with the Tribunal or maybe some Defence team. They provided everything they had. Maybe there was a rule that allowed them not to provide it. They could have said perhaps, We don't have it, because as you said, it has not been register, it is not in the central archives, and there is absolutely no paper trail of its existence. However; they seem to have been conscientious and to have provided the documents as they were drafted in 1999. Of course, you can check the authenticity of these documents and you can also check it by comparing what is written here with the contents of the document that is official and that is titled "Brief," "Informacija" in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was waiting for the translation. Yeah. The -- the "Informacija" then is the more formal document that would have a signature and a stamp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And everything that's contained in this briefing note, this informal document, would have been incorporated verbatim in that final document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not strictly verbatim. Not necessarily. Maybe some other elements relevant to the units which received this information would be added, but most of it would be in the document entitled "Informacija" with the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this the appropriate time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, we need another break at this stage for half an hour. Could you again leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we please show the witness Exhibit Number 3D898. General, coming up on your screen will be the briefing from the 28th of March, 1999. And I'd like to look at paragraph 4, which yesterday we heard said recommendations would be made for a forceful entry into Kosovo and Metohija in the event it's evaluated, our forces were built up to 50.000 and if the number of refugees reached 500.000. If the situation got to the point where there were 500.000 refugees, wouldn't you agree that that would be a humanitarian catastrophe of a sufficient magnitude to perhaps call for entry by NATO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, as we well know, airstrikes were already on. The war had already started. And this information is something we had received as one of the possible assessments. That was true as far as we were able to analyse. Namely, that NATO had evaluated or decided that if the number of refugees grew to 500.000, that could be cause for a forceful entry into Kosovo. But as we know, it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the next sentence that wasn't read yesterday says: "This is why the response to the provocations of the so-called KLA should be completed as soon as possible." And it's a fact, sir, isn't it, that during the first two weeks of the war the VJ, the Pristina Corps, in joint activities with the MUP, were fully engaged in trying to get rid of as many KLA as they could, to clear the area out in the event of a NATO ground attack? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the war had already begun, it was logical that the forces engaged in the defence of the country should try to create a situation as favourable to themselves as possible, and one of them could be the proposition you just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to the next page of this document, please. And, General, the last paragraph there we see the comment: "I support Mr. Grahovac's suggestion for conducting a strategic military assessment as soon as possible, if possible in the presence of the members of the Supreme Defence Council." So was that presentation done for the Supreme Defence Council sometime on or after the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Analysing that situation which was developing rather adversely, we were looking for ways to deal with it. And one of the measures is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, I'm short on time. That's a fairly straight forward question. Was that presentation done for the Supreme Defence Council? If you know.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The monitoring was done, but not for the Supreme Defence Council, because they were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They were not present at all during the war? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the presentation of that analysis on the 9th of April, none of the Supreme Defence Council was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that meeting on the 9th of April, we've seen the collegium minutes for that day, and General Ojdanic talks near the end of that session about having all that material prepared so he can take it to the Supreme Command. You recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I don't recall every word, but it was logical that after such a serious analysis the material would be made available to the Supreme Defence Council. But I can't say whether General Ojdanic really submit it and to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In the next exhibit, 3D906, please, there's a reference in this briefing, General, to an announcement on CNN. Did you guys during the war watch CNN to see what they were reporting about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We watched everything we could, including media we used as indicators of what might happen. But, of course, we did not attach absolute importance to the media. We didn't consider that everything that was reported in them was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you watch CNN and BBC?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, CNN, BBC. We listened to the Voice of America and various other TV and radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand the point about perhaps not giving much weight to some or much of what they said, but you were aware that they were fairly daily reports about thousands of Kosovo Albanian civilian refugees pouring out of Kosovo and Metohija during those first few weeks of the war? Is that correct? That was being reported by them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were quite a lot of reports about that in the foreign media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 3D911, the next one I'd like to show you, Mr. Visnjic asked you about a diplomatic initiative and then a second proposal that was made regarding post or points for refugees. Do you find that? I'm not sure if that's on the first page. I think it's at the next page, where you have "Conclusions and proposals." Could we go to the next page. I'm sorry. And in connection with that proposal, it is stated: "In order to avoid being demonised in the media." I suggest, General, that was an even greater concern than whether the refugees left Kosovo or not. It was the way it appeared and was being presented in the media that you were most concerned about. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the media, there was, of course, correct information, but there were also exaggerations and incorrect information which we called "media demonisation" in those wartime conditions. The idea of organising those points was calculated to mitigate the refugee problem, to provide assistance in an organised manner for the refugees, and change the media picture so that it would no longer be unfavourable as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that proposal ever actually carried out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that something was done in part. I know that in those days General Pavkovic called me up on one occasion and asked me about the refugees and what I thought should be done. And I think they did something, but I can't give you details. I'm not sure precisely what they did and how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last item there says: "Likewise, the insinuations concerning the replacement of the commander of the 2nd Army could be refuted." What was that issue about the replacement of the commander of the 2nd Army? Who was that and why was he being replaced at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Army was General Radoslav Martinovic. He was replaced by General Milorad Obradovic. Why the change was made? To be quite honest, I really don't know, because that was within the competence of the chief of the General Staff. As in many other cases, there were various media speculations about it, about why he was replaced. My idea was that a truthful communique would put an end to the speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you just said you didn't quite know why, so how could you know what the truthful answer was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take it upon myself to draft the truthful communique. I expected that those who had replaced him would provide the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who had replaced him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced by General Milorad Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who ordered that replacement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The change was at the level of generals, was within the competence of the President of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The President of the FRY; right? Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, because the interpreters did not catch everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Milosevic was President at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was the one who replaced the commander of the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, he signed the ordinance, which is the document regulating the replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I don't understand the answer, then. Who did replace him if it was not Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules, the chief of the General Staff proposes the replacement or one of the members of the Supreme Defence Council, but the President is the one authorised to sign the document, which is called an ordinance, whereby such a replacement at the level of the rank of general is regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So it wouldn't have happened unless Mr. Milosevic signed that ordinance; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't have happened. I didn't see the ordinance by President Milosevic myself, so I can't say exactly what the mechanism of that particular replacement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked about some information regarding the possibility of airstrikes and you talked about the credibility of NATO was emphasised as a reason. It's possible that the credibility of NATO was linked to events on the ground and most of all with what they referred to as "the humanitarian catastrophe." Now, I wanted to ask you about, I think this is from the collegium meeting on the 9th of April. NATO credibility relates back to the events in October of 1998, doesn't it? Because wasn't there an ACTORD that had been issued and then Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Holbrooke reached the agreement at the end of October, so NATO backed off bombing at that time. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a document ACTORD, but it was not completely abolished. It was only suspended. It remained in force, but it was suspended, as far as we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be fair to say that having gone really to the brink or up to the last minute back in October, NATO couldn't simply say okay again if Mr. Milosevic now said, Oh, I'm sorry, I will -- I will stop doing what I'm doing and I'll do everything I promised to do in October? I mean, how many times could that process be repeated?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to comment on this, because I was not in the NATO structures nor was I close to President Milosevic, so I could not know what the relations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that. I guess I was asking the question because you -- you are an experienced professional soldier, and I think you probably understand about the use of force and the threat of force and that you can only -- you can only threaten so many times before eventually you have to actually carry it out or you have no credibility any more. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Credibility. Yes, we often came across that, because the military and other representatives of NATO often referred to the credibility of NATO in the days leading up to the airstrikes, about preserving NATO's credibility. As a counterargument, we always said that NATO's credibility would be best preserved if the problem were solved without the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Exhibit 3D955 from the 12th of May, you told us about -- you were exploring every option at your disposal at that time and trying to find a peaceful solution and a way to end the war. And one of the proposals here from you is the issue of the return of the refugees and even the possible withdrawal of VJ units to garrisons away from Kosovo. Proposals are great, but can you tell me -- can you point to any concrete steps that the VJ took regarding the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I wasn't on the ground there and I was interested in the problem of refugees more from the point of view of the foreign factors and trying to lessen the negative influence of that. But as to what was actually happening on the ground, I couldn't say. The proposals I put forward were sincere and their intention was to start solving the problem, not just the issue of refugees but also cessation of the airstrikes and everything else that was causing the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we look at 3D753. You -- you told us about this yesterday, General. And this -- this is a document I think you told us was the VJ proclamation about having the Albanians return. Mr. Visnjic asked you if this was the document that was issued by the army, and your answer then at page 16818 was: "I can't tell you now with any precision whether this is the document, whether it contains all the elements, but I do know that such a proclamation was made." This looks like a draft to me. I don't see a -- there's no signature on it and I don't see a stamp or a date. Do you know when this was created and who created this particular document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was created around that date. It was broadcast on the media. That can be checked. But as I said, I can't vouch for the authenticity of the text itself, because I didn't work on it myself, so I can't say how authentic it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you show us or can you point us to where there's evidence, hard evidence that it was actually circulated to any of the persons that might have an interest in it or be affected by it? First of all, where is -- where is the version in the Albanian language? Is there one?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that. Of course, there should have been. But whether there was or wasn't, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a general question about the intelligence information you got, because you gave us a lot of examples of some of the kinds of information you had. But wouldn't you agree with me that a lot of information that -- that you received wasn't accurate? It didn't -- it didn't pan out. It didn't prove to be accurate. That's -- that's the nature of intelligence, isn't it? I mean, a lot of things you hear and are given to you just don't prove to be true.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that, generally speaking. And in addition to the information presented to the staff of the superior -- of the Supreme Command, we receive dozens of other pieces of information which we assessed as being unrealistic or unimportant and we did not present those. We didn't include them in the briefings that we delivered to the users of our briefings. So what you say certainly applies to any intelligence service in the world. Not all information received is 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It seems that I saw one -- one item in one of the intelligence briefings about -- there was a report about some sort of bomber was being painted in Croatia to look like a VJ plane with a plan to bomb civilians in Kosovo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember an information -- a piece of information to that effect which proved to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You would agree with me that seems pretty far-fetched, doesn't it? As a practical matter, how was that going to work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this distance in time, it might seem exaggerated, but we were in the middle of a war. All sorts of things were happening. Emotions were involved, not just rational criteria. We feared various threats, and that's why we responded as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I -- I hope never to be in that position myself. All right. I won't ask you about a couple other examples. I did want to ask you about a few things that were brought up this morning. Mr. Visnjic asked you about whether you'd ever heard about a plan to expel Albanians, and you told us that, you know, you would attend those meetings and you never heard such ideas at any of the meetings you attended. But you did hear the media reports and you probably heard complaints from NGOs which included victim accounts about Kosovar Albanians being expelled by FRY security forces and including having their identity documents destroyed and the license plates taken off their vehicles before they were forced across the border. You were aware that there were allegations about that kind of thing in March and April of 1999, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the media and in other ways, such information did go round, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One answer you gave I wasn't clear about. You were asked some questions about the Supreme Command. And you made the point that "Supreme Command" is not defined in your laws. And I agree, it doesn't appear to be anywhere in the Constitution or the Law on Defence or the Law on the Army. And your answer is reported in the transcript as being - and I quote here, General - it says: "My belief is that it existed and that it should have included members of the Supreme Defence Council, the Prime Minister, the Defence Minister, the Minister of the Interior, the Finance Minister possibly, and perhaps some other high-ranking officials of the state." Is that correct? It was your belief that the Supreme Command did exist during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the translation was, but if it's as you say, it's incorrect. I didn't say it existed. I said "if it had existed," "had it existed," it would most probably have the structure I spoke about. But I didn't say that it did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... To that. Wasn't there a Supreme Command that existed during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normatively, it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain for me what that means, "normatively."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that in the constitution and in the laws you mentioned there is no mention anywhere of the existence of a Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. And -- and we've talked about a lot of things and a lot of formalities. But as you said in answer to other questions, during wartime things are different. And some things that -- that are not on the books and some things that perhaps should not happen actually do exist and do happen in real life. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, one of the -- I'm sorry, I guess you have to answer out loud. I didn't ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a question of philosophy and logic, and I can't answer it with a "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Does that mean you have to say "no"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what you're asking me. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we know that during peacetime the President of the FRY, Mr. Milosevic, commanded the army in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, who we understand were the Presidents of Serbia and Montenegro, that is, Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Djukanovic. You agree with me so far?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that's what it says in the Constitution. It's the Supreme Defence Council, or rather, the President of the Republic that commands the army in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And the Constitution and the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army say that the -- the President of the Republic of Yugoslavia commanded the army in wartime as well, and that was to be in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So during the -- during the wartime, 78 or 79 days, we know Mr. Milosevic was the Supreme Commander. So how did he command in accordance with the Constitution and those laws unless he was acting in conjunction with Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Djukanovic? Was he violating the law?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you stated quite correctly that the President was in command of the army in peace and in war based on decisions by the Supreme Defence Council. Secondly, I think the second thing you said is not quite correct, that is, that Milosevic was the Supreme Commander. In formal terms, he may have performed the duty of Supreme Commander, but he's nowhere defined as Supreme Commander in the legislation. As for the third part of your question, whether he agreed on his commands with the members of the Supreme Defence Council, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're being very formal with me, General. I understand that there wasn't in the Constitution that title "Supreme Commander." But, as a matter of fact, isn't that a term of general usage by generals and by others that Mr. Milosevic during the war was referred to as the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's how it appears in many VJ documents. And we also have in evidence some VJ documents that refer to "the Supreme Command," which it's the Prosecution's position is basically the wartime equivalent of the Supreme Defence Council and included Mr. Milutinovic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that this is true, because I'm not a constitutional legal expert, so I cannot clarify whether or not the Supreme Defence Council is equivalent to the Supreme Command. As I've already said, in my opinion and after analysis of examples in other countries, had a Supreme Command existed, it would have had to contain some additional elements, not just the three men in the Supreme Defence Council. But that's just my opinion. As I said, I'm no constitutional expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's okay. We've had one of those. But you were there, General, on the ground and in the Supreme Command Staff headquarters. And we've seen in the April 9th collegium General Ojdanic referring to having documents prepared to take to the Supreme Command, not just the Supreme Commander but the Supreme Command. I agree with you that makes sense that during the wartime the Supreme Defence Council might be expanded to include others. After all, it's a war. But would it not at least include the Supreme Defence Council members, that is, the Presidents of Montenegro and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in our state, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as it was then, had everything been set up the way it should have been set up, as it was set up in democratic countries of the world, that would probably have been the case. But as you know, this did not happen. In other words, nowhere was it specified that the Supreme Command existed and the composition of that command was not specified and neither were the powers of that command specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily have to be written down for something to exist and function, though, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, when was it you became chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I took over the -- the duty on the 25th of June, 2002, and until the end -- but I was not specific enough. Until the end of December, I was the stand-in for the chief and only then did I become a fully-fledged chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have some brief cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In -- in regard to what, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mostly it's in regard to the Joint Command issue that was raised by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bakrac, were you going to raise something as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't see Mr. Ackerman, who precedes me. I have two short questions that were raised in cross-examination related to the documents on the Joint Command and another document, but that will be very brief. I will just be showing the witness one sentence and I will have two quick questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any problem with these requests, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Carry on, please, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, you were shown a couple of documents by Mr. Hannis that there was quite lot of discussion about. That's P1487, which was that document where Ojdanic makes suggestions regarding an order, that purports to be a Joint Command order. And then you saw the order that is purported to be the Joint Command order. That was 1878. When you looked at 1878, which was clear that if it was anything, it was an order of the Pristina Corps regarding a prospective action; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the question I have for you, because you have been the -- the number-one guy, the chief of the General Staff: The -- the decisions about how to go out -- about carrying out your orders by the army commander and the corps commanders are pretty much their decisions. They decide which units they want to use to carry out those orders, and so forth. And it's not a good idea for someone at your level to interfere with those decisions. That's pretty much their job to make those decisions and carry out your orders; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. But a superior may suggest to the subordinate how a task should be carried out, if there is any need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But if you see an order like that one contained in P1878 and with your broader experience you think there may be a better way to approach that task, it's totally appropriate for you to make suggestions to that corps commander or to a 3rd Army commander about how the matter should be pursued, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a superior at a level of the General Staff does not present any suggestions to the commander at the level of the 3rd -- of the command of a corps, but he issues an order regulating all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But once you see what it is the corps commander is proposing to do, there wouldn't be anything wrong with you suggesting that he might consider doing it a different way, would there? Wouldn't that be consistent with your experience and your job? So that when General Ojdanic in this case was making suggestions, he wasn't saying, You're my superior. He was just saying, Here are some better ways to do it maybe.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, but in the majority of cases, the communication went in the other way and the usual type of relation is the command relations. You issue and you receive orders. But, of course, there could be suggestions, provided that the subordinate commander is given enough leeway to set up an operation or an action that he conceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I have another document now I want to show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on to that. Have you any experience, Mr. Krga, of seeing a document headed "Suggestions" or making suggestions in the way that P1487 did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to say that I don't recall ever seeing any such document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next document I'd like you to look at is 3D692. 3D692 is a document dated 29 May, 1999. And if you look at the very beginning of it, you see what it's saying is that pursuant to your order -- it's addressed to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. Pursuant to your order, a team inspection of the command and part of the units of the Pristina Corps was carried out between -- I can't tell exactly what that says, because I can't see it well. But in May of 1999. It was probably 23 and 26 and it's a mistake there. And then if you look at the final page, you'll see that it was signed by Colonel General Velickovic. Now, who was Colonel General Velickovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel General Velickovic was the commander of the air force and air defence until October 1998. After that, he became the Deputy Defence Minister, and then sometime in mid-April 1999 - in other words, during the war - he replaced General Grahovac at the post according to the wartime establishment that was the chief of the administration for air force and air defence. During the war, on the 1st of June, 1999, he was killed at a position of a rocket unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at this time in May, in the late days in May, he was sent down to Kosovo apparently to conduct this inspection. Why would he have been the person chosen to do that? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I need to object at this point. I'm not sure how this arises from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm getting there. It will be in maybe the next question. But this is just setting background --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- For the information I'm trying to get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the question? Why would he have been sent to do this by the commanding general?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In such cases, you had two options: Either he himself had given this initiative saying that he would like to tour some units, that he was either the superior commander or he was responsible for; or he could have been ordered to do so by the chief of the General Staff if he was deemed to be necessary. In this specific case, I don't know whether he had been ordered or whether this was an initiative on his part, that he wanted to go and visit that installation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the very beginning, I think you'll see that he was ordered to do so by the chief of the General Staff. I think that appears at page 1. And rather than go there now, what I really want you to look at is paragraph 11 in the context of the Prosecution's contention that there was a Joint Command operating in Kosovo at this time. So if we'll get paragraph 11 up on the screen maybe. It's probably around page 4 of the document. There it is. One of the things he reports in this report is that: "There is no single command over all the forces in the zone of responsibility. All contacts with the units of the MUP are established by agreement, which is often disobeyed, especially at the lower levels." And it goes on to talk about the relationships between the VJ and the MUP and basically how bad they are; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is written in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that certainly doesn't look like a situation where there was one command over the MUP and the VJ and they already operating together in a Joint Command, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with reference to the date of May 29th?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's the date of the document. Yes. 29 May of 1999 is the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It really is part of your argument, Mr. Ackerman, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm going on now to a final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony today, page 76, line 20 you were asked about some issues regarding refugees apparently coming back into Kosovo. And you said that "Pavkovic called to ask about refugees." Do you remember about when it was that you call the call from General Pavkovic in that regard?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the date, but I think it was sometime in early April, the first few days of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the concern by General Pavkovic was that somehow arrangements needed to be made to take care of these people, make sure they were clothed and housed and fed and things of that nature and what should he do about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way I assessed it, that this was also new to him and that he was asking us whether he knew what was happening, what the basic causes were, and what should be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is a transcript -- in the transcript again, it's 93, 20. I believe the witness says "he was asking us whether he knew what was happening." "He."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 93 -- not 20. Which line is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is 20, "whether we knew what was happening." And that's what I heard too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 23? It's not line --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 93, line 20. It says: "And that he was asking us whether we [Realtime transcript read in error "he"] knew what was happening." Instead of "he knew what was happening," it should be said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "we knew."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness said "we knew what was happening."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Krga. I have a couple of questions for you, very brief questions. The Prosecutor showed you document P1999, and there is no need for us to have us back -- have it back on our screens. This is an analysis of the command of the 249th Brigade regarding an action in the village of Kabas dated the 17th of March, 1999. My question to you is whether you know that this village of Kabas where this action was undertaken is actually in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you off the top of my head where this village actually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you perhaps know that this action was announced in advance to OSCE?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you don't know those details. Let me now move on to the next document. That's P1966. And could we please have it up on e-court. That's the order of the Joint Command regarding Malo Kosovo. And could we please have page 2 of this document. General, in order to be entirely fair to you, you spoke about this document and also about that addendum to this document. Could you please look at paragraph 4, where it says "Decision," and the last sentence just above where it says paragraph 5, "Readiness." Is the readiness for this task actually defined here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with our rules, paragraph 4, "Decision," has to determine -- usually determines the readiness deadline for the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The fact that the readiness is not defined here, does that not explain what you actually told us that a corps commander cannot amend a decision that was issued by a superior command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally. Had a Joint Command existed as a command superior to the Pristina Corps, then the Pristina Corps commander could not have amended their decision. He could only implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And it is quite obvious why there is this amendment, because the readiness is not defined in the first document. Is that how we should read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is quite obvious that the same command drafted both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything arising from these, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, only that I would -- with regard to the last question, I would direct the Court to P1967, which is the amendment to the order and on the second page under item 4, it does have a time listed for the readiness for combat as being 0600 hours on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic. How long are you likely to be with re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have very brief re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Everyone at the moment indulging us to try and insist in completing this evidence today. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I ask some questions, I would like to draw the Court's attention to the document that was mentioned by Mr. Bakrac. That's P1999, dated the 18th of March, 1999. Mr. Hannis asked the witness about this document, and it was put to the witness that this is one of the events that caused concern for General Dimitrijevic at the collegium meeting held on the same date, the 18th of March, 1999. That's P938. Your Honours, I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that in document P1999, the time when this document is indicated is -- the time when this document was sent is indicated and you -- when this document was actually sent to the Pristina Corps staff, and you can see from the other document that the meeting of the collegium was held on the same day but substantially earlier than that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, Mr. Hannis asked you several questions about the possibilities to launch misinformation, that one side may try to misinform the other side. And then he asked you about the credibility of the information that you received, and he gave you an example that, a Croatian plane that was purportedly to be used to bomb Kosovo. During the examination-in-chief, I asked you regarding Defence Exhibit 3D43 -- 635. That was the assessment in -- that you did in February. But now I want to ask you: From where you sit now, how would you evaluate the assessments that the Army of Yugoslavia had before and during the airstrikes? Airstrikes in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would perhaps be biased if I were to evaluate the work of the service that I headed, but I think that the developments, the events that followed those assessments, often unfortunately confirmed the credibility of most of the information that we had and the assessments that we had done. I say "unfortunately" because most of those -- those information and assessments were negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis brought up Exhibit P935. That's the collegium meeting in March. And he mentioned what General Curcin said about the reinforcements and the deployment of units in and around Kosovo. General, on the 11th of March, do you know about the increasing the strength of the ground forces of NATO in Macedonia? We know that there were 1.850 at the beginning there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at first there were 1.850. Then in February, there were about 5.000 of them. And then that number increased to 12.500 in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yet another question in this respect. Mr. Hannis mentioned the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, the October agreements. I think that's how we should call them. Do you know that at least in one of those agreements the right of the Army of Yugoslavia to self-defence is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, how is it that you know that the Holbrooke agreement contained a reference to self-defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean the Holbrooke agreement. I meant -- I was referring to a decision of the Supreme Defence Council from that time period that made reference to the fact that we wanted peace but if the army came under attack, that it is entitled to take every measure defend itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to ask something else, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I've already been told. I didn't think that it was irrelevant, but I mentioned several decisions from October. I first said "the Holbrooke thing," the Holbrooke Agreement," and then I mentioned several agreements from October, but I don't think that it was recorded in the translation. But I was actually referring to P395. That was the Naumann agreement, the Clark-Naumann Agreement, P395. If I may be allowed, perhaps I could ask just one question to clarify that in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can read it for ourselves, can we not? If you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to give you the context, just so that you see what I was driving at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, had the Army of Yugoslavia not carried out certain preparations or taken some measures of self-defence and self-protection before the airstrikes began, what would be your assessment? What would be its fate? What would have been its fate from the 24th of March onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to give you a one-sentence answer to that question, but its fate would have been bad. That's for sure. And from the point of view of the actions launched by the KLA and the airstrikes that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give your evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the you should.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for tomorrow morning's planning purposes, we'll simply submit a -- we'll put in a written submission to the Radinovic expert report comments by the Prosecutor. We'll waive oral argument. We'll have it in this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. And we have one -- we anticipate one witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already abandoned plans to leave Mr. Radinovic, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, we wait for a decision and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's -- it is still possible that he may give his evidence in chief tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, hardly. Hardly. In -- in view of the time we have at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When then do you envisage leading him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, what I was going to say- and I missed the translation there - we have this whole -- all this stuff about these intercepts. I think it would be -- I mean, certainly not until after the break. We have the intercept materials to sort out. We have the decision that Your Honours will make on whether or not there's any merit to the Prosecution's objections, to his report. And I just see no chance at all of his testifying tomorrow. It just -- it's just not in the cards, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the -- the intercepts are really speculation at the moment. You don't know how they may impact on your evidence. Once you do, then it would be possible for you to lead the necessary evidence to -- to handle their impact. So it may be a bit premature to abandon your plans, but it's a matter for you to decide at this stage. It may have an impact on the time available to you after the break for the important evidence of Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. I think we're going to -- Mr. Visnjic and I both agree that the important thing is what the lead counsel agrees to, of course. But we do agree that we're going to be very summary on the last two witnesses. These will not be lengthy witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By that -- by "the last two witnesses," you're referring to Radinovic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And General Ojdanic. Right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, the Bench are very grateful to everyone who has insisted today by continuing to work beyond the normal time. We're very grateful for the result that that has achieved, which is to enable us to concentrate tomorrow on the final witness for this session. So we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
